### Hold it → side
1) **Up/down** → the flat, concave **plafond** faces down to the talus
[[FIG: Fig 8.1, 8.2 · 8.01

8.03.t: Talus Blood Supply — the Real Question
8.03.b:
| Artery | From | Supplies |
|---|---|---|
| **Artery of the tarsal canal** | Posterior tibial | **Main supply of the body**  |
[[FIG: Fig 8.6 · 8.03
| **Deltoid branch** | Artery of the tarsal canal | **Medial body** → saved if the deltoid is kept |
| **Artery of the sinus tarsi** | Peroneal perforating + dorsalis pedis | Neck and lateral body |
| **Superomedial / dorsal neck branches** | Dorsalis pedis | **Head and neck** |

- Share by MRI → **PT (posterior tibial) 47% · anterior tibial 36% · peroneal 17%**
  [[FIG: Fig 8.7 · 8.03
- New **medial neck branch** → cut by a standard anteromedial approach

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "Blood supply of the talus"
- No muscle, 60% cartilage → vessels enter at **neck, sinus tarsi, tarsal canal, medial body, posterior process**
- Main → **artery of the tarsal canal** (posterior tibial) → body; its **deltoid branch** → medial body
- **Artery of the sinus tarsi** (peroneal + dorsalis pedis) → lateral body; **dorsalis pedis** → head and neck
- Canal + sinus form a **sling under the neck** → retrograde flow → a neck fracture threatens the body
- Hawkins I → IV → AVN (avascular necrosis) **10% → 100%** (table below) · **Hawkins sign** = alive (Netter)

| Hawkins type | What is displaced | AVN |
|---|---|---|
| I | Undisplaced neck | 10% |
| II | + subtalar dislocation | 40% |
| III | + ankle (tibiotalar) dislocation | 90% |
| IV | + talonavicular dislocation | 100% |

- **Hawkins sign** → subchondral lucency at 6–8 weeks = no AVN
- Talar neck exposure → **dual approach**, never strip the deltoid → 8B

8.06.b:
### The mortise
- **Hinge** → **DF (dorsiflexion) 20°, PF (plantar flexion) 50°** · **only the talus** of the tarsals enters the mortise
  [[FIG: Fig 8.23 · 8.06
- DF → the fibula **rotates and widens** the mortise round the wide front of the talus → **cast in neutral, never in plantar flexion**

### Syndesmosis — four ligaments
[[FIG: Fig 8.24, 8.25, 8.26, 8.27 · 8.06
| Ligament | Note |
|---|---|
| **AITFL** | **Torn first** in external rotation |
| **PITFL** | Strong; avulses the **Volkmann** fragment instead of tearing |
| **ITL** (inferior transverse) | Deep part of the PITFL → **labrum** of the posterior plafond |
| **IOL** (interosseous) | Lowest thickening of the IOM (interosseous membrane) |

- Syndesmotic injury = "high ankle sprain"

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "Fibular fracture level and the syndesmosis" (Nagah p16)
- **Weber A** → below the plafond → syndesmosis **intact** → stable (lateral ligament equivalent)
- **Weber B** → at the level (trans-syndesmotic) → syndesmosis **may** be torn → stress view decides
- **Weber C** → above → syndesmosis **torn** up to the fracture level, IOM torn → unstable
- **Maisonneuve** → proximal fibula + whole syndesmosis + deltoid / medial malleolus → look up the leg (Netter)
- Rule → **the higher the fibular fracture, the more syndesmosis is torn**

- Decide by the fracture **level** + a **stress / weight-bearing view**, not the line's direction (Nagah p16)
- Lauge-Hansen → **supination–external rotation** (commonest) = Weber B → torn in stages **AITFL → fibula → PITFL / Volkmann → medial** · supination starts **lateral**, pronation starts **medial**

EXAM PEARL — "Why dorsiflex the ankle when you put in the syndesmotic screw?" (Nagah p16)
- Classic → maximal DF puts the **wide front of the talus** in the mortise → the screw cannot narrow it
- Fixing in plantar flexion did **not** limit DF (Tornetta 2001)
- Say → "**dorsiflexion is the traditional safety step; accurate reduction matters more**"

8.08.b:
### Subtalar & Chopart
- Subtalar → **inversion / eversion** only · **sinus tarsi** → **interosseous talocalcaneal + cervical** ligaments
- Chopart → **talonavicular** (ball-and-socket) + **calcaneocuboid** (saddle)
  [[FIG: Fig 8.35 · 8.08
- **Heel eversion → axes parallel → supple** midfoot; **inversion → axes cross → rigid** lever (toe-off)
- **Bifurcate ligament** → anterior calcaneal process to navicular + cuboid; avulsion = anterior process fracture

### Lisfranc (tarsometatarsal) joint
- **No ligament between the 1st and 2nd MT bases** → the Lisfranc ligament does that job
  [[FIG: Fig 8.36, 8.37, 8.38 · 8.08
- 2nd MT base **recessed** between the cuneiforms = **keystone** of the transverse (Roman) arch
- Middle column → **least** motion → fuse freely · lateral column → **most** → keep it mobile
- **Fleck sign** (2nd MT base avulsion) or a **>2 mm** 1st–2nd base gap → unstable Lisfranc (Nagah p10)

PITFALL — strongest Lisfranc layer
- Netter → plantar strongest; OB Foot + Johnson 2008 → **interosseous** strongest
- Say → "**the interosseous Lisfranc ligament is strongest, dorsal weakest** → injuries open dorsally"

HIGH YIELD — what is at risk, by region
- **Anteromedial** portal (medial to **TA**, joint line) → **saphenous nerve + great saphenous vein** → safest, made first
- **Anterolateral** portal (lateral to **peroneus tertius**), distal fibula plate → **SPN** (intermediate dorsal cutaneous)
- **Posterolateral** portal (Achilles edge, **1 cm above the fibular tip**), lateral calcaneus, 5th MT, Achilles → **sural nerve + small saphenous vein**
- Medial hindfoot (calcaneal pin, tarsal tunnel, posteromedial portal) → **PT bundle** + medial calcaneal nerve
- Dorsal midfoot (anterocentral portal, Lisfranc approach) → **DPN + dorsalis pedis** over the 1st–2nd interspace

- Extensile lateral calcaneal flap → carries the **lateral calcaneal artery** (→ Arteries)
- Approach-by-approach dangers → 8B

8.17.b:
| Test | Why it works (anatomy) | Trap |
|---|---|---|
| **Anterior drawer** | **20° plantar flexion** → ATFL tight, narrow back of the talus free to slide (OB Foot) | Done in DF → mortise locks → false negative |
| **Talar tilt** | Inversion in DF/neutral → CFL tight (Netter) | Subtalar inversion mimics a tilt |
| **Squeeze test** | Squeezing the mid-calf springs the fibula from the tibia → loads the syndesmosis | Fibular fracture also hurts |
| **External rotation (Kleiger)** | Rotating the talus pushes the fibula out → AITFL + deep deltoid | Pain medial = deltoid, anterolateral = syndesmosis |
| **Thompson** | Squeezing the calf shortens the triceps → plantar flexion only if the Achilles is in continuity (Netter) | Intact plantaris / FHL → active PF still possible |

[[FIG: Fig 8.87, 8.88, 8.89 · 8.17

- **Single heel rise** → TP inverts and locks the hindfoot → heel goes into varus; fails in TP dysfunction (Netter)
- **Too-many-toes** → forefoot abduction in flatfoot → more toes seen from behind; compare sides
- **Coleman block** → 1st ray off the block removes the PL-driven forefoot pronation (Netter) → heel corrects = flexible hindfoot, forefoot-driven
- **Silfverskiöld** → knee flexed slackens gastrocnemius (crosses the knee), not soleus (OB Foot) → more DF with knee bent = gastrocnemius tight
